raw_text:
Cardiac amyloidosis is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy caused by extracellular myocardial deposition of misfolded proteins, producing restrictive physiology, atrial and conduction disease, and ultimately heart failure. Contemporary practice is dominated by two etiologies: immunoglobulin light-chain amyloidosis (AL), a plasma-cell dyscrasia that requires urgent hematologic therapy, and transthyretin amyloidosis (ATTR), either wild-type (ATTRwt) or variant (ATTRv) [1–4]. The former may progress over weeks to months because circulating light chains are directly cardiotoxic, whereas ATTR usually evolves more slowly through destabilization of the transthyretin tetramer and myocardial fibril deposition [4].

Recognition has increased because noninvasive pathways have revealed disease in older adults previously labeled as having hypertensive heart disease, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, or heart failure with preserved ejection fraction (HFpEF). ATTRwt is particularly enriched in elderly men, in patients with HFpEF and increased wall thickness, and in those with aortic stenosis; bilateral carpal tunnel syndrome, lumbar stenosis, biceps tendon rupture, neuropathy, unexplained proteinuria, low-flow aortic stenosis, or discordant low-voltage electrocardiography should heighten suspicion [13–17]. Registry data also show important genotype–phenotype heterogeneity, including the p.Val142Ile variant, which disproportionately affects individuals of African ancestry and often presents with predominant cardiomyopathy [15].

Diagnosis should proceed in parallel rather than serial fashion, because missing AL amyloidosis can be fatal. Initial evaluation includes electrocardiography, echocardiography with strain, cardiac biomarkers, renal assessment, and monoclonal-protein testing with serum free light chains plus serum and urine immunofixation [1,2]. Echocardiography typically shows increased ventricular wall thickness, biatrial enlargement, restrictive filling, valve thickening, pericardial effusion, and reduced longitudinal strain with relative apical sparing, although apical sparing is neither perfectly sensitive nor specific [7]. Cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) adds tissue characterization: diffuse subendocardial or transmural late gadolinium enhancement, abnormal gadolinium kinetics, elevated native T1, and expanded extracellular volume quantify amyloid burden and carry prognostic information [8,9].

The diagnostic inflection point has been bone-avid scintigraphy. In a patient with a compatible phenotype, grade 2–3 myocardial uptake on technetium-labeled pyrophosphate, DPD, or HMDP scintigraphy, combined with absence of monoclonal protein, is sufficient to diagnose ATTR cardiomyopathy without biopsy [5,6]. If monoclonal protein is present, if uptake is equivocal, or if the phenotype is atypical, tissue confirmation and accurate amyloid typing are essential; laser microdissection with mass spectrometry is now the reference method when immunohistochemistry is inconclusive [26,27]. Genetic testing is mandatory after an ATTR diagnosis to distinguish ATTRwt from ATTRv and to guide family screening.

Risk stratification is biomarker-driven. In AL amyloidosis, troponin, NT-proBNP, and the involved–uninvolved free-light-chain difference define Mayo staging; serial NT-proBNP and hematologic response correlate strongly with survival [10–12]. ATTR staging systems use NT-proBNP with either troponin or renal function, reflecting the combined effects of myocardial burden and cardiorenal reserve [13,14].

Management combines supportive cardiovascular care with precursor-directed therapy. Diuretics are the mainstay for congestion; hypotension and autonomic dysfunction often limit beta-blockers, renin–angiotensin inhibitors, and calcium-channel blockers. Atrial fibrillation, conduction disease, and intracardiac thrombus are common; anticoagulation is generally favored for atrial fibrillation irrespective of conventional risk scores, and rhythm-control procedures require careful thrombus exclusion [24,25].

For AL cardiomyopathy, treatment is a hematologic emergency aimed at rapid light-chain suppression. Daratumumab plus bortezomib, cyclophosphamide, and dexamethasone has become a frontline standard, improving hematologic complete response and organ outcomes; bortezomib-based regimens remain central, with selected fit patients considered for autologous stem-cell transplantation or sequential cardiac and hematologic strategies [22,23]. For ATTR cardiomyopathy, tafamidis established transthyretin stabilization as disease-modifying therapy by reducing mortality and cardiovascular hospitalization [18]. Acoramidis, another stabilizer, and RNA-silencing therapies such as patisiran and vutrisiran have expanded the therapeutic landscape, with trials showing benefits on functional capacity, biomarkers, quality of life, and clinical events [19–21,30]. Future challenges include earlier detection, equitable access to expensive therapies, comparative sequencing or combination strategies, and validated measures of amyloid regression [28,29].
